facts.statement: The Rodrigues parrot (Necropsittacus rodricanus) was an extinct parrot species endemic to the island of Rodrigues.
facts.quote: The Rodrigues parrot or Leguat's parrot (Necropsittacus rodricanus) is an extinct species of parrot that was endemic to the Mascarene island of Rodrigues.

facts.statement: The Rodrigues parrot was last mentioned in 1761 and likely went extinct soon after due to introduced predators, deforestation, and human hunting.
facts.quote: The species was last mentioned in 1761, and probably became extinct soon after, perhaps due to a combination of predation by introduced animals, deforestation, and hunting by humans.

facts.statement: The Rodrigues parrot was first mentioned by French traveler François Leguat in his 1708 memoir, A New Voyage to the East Indies.
facts.quote: Birds thought to be the Rodrigues parrot were first mentioned by the French traveler François Leguat in his 1708 memoir, A New Voyage to the East Indies.

facts.statement: In 1867, French zoologist Alphonse Milne-Edwards described subfossil bones of the Rodrigues parrot received via British ornithologist Alfred Newton.
facts.quote: In 1867, the French zoologist Alphonse Milne-Edwards described subfossil bird bones from Rodrigues he had received via the British ornithologist Alfred Newton, which had been excavated under the supervision of his brother, Colonial Secretary Edward Newton.

facts.statement: Alphonse Milne-Edwards scientifically described and named the species Psittacus rodricanus based on a fragmentary upper beak.
facts.quote: Based on this beak, he scientifically described and named the new species Psittacus rodricanus.

facts.statement: In 1873, Milne-Edwards moved the species to the genus Necropsittacus after receiving more complete beak remains.
facts.quote: After receiving a more complete upper and lower beak which he thought showed the bird to be close to the parrot genus Palaeornis, Milne-Edwards moved the species to its own genus Necropsittacus in 1873

facts.statement: Subfossil remains of the Rodrigues parrot have been found in caves on the Plaine Corail and in Caverne Tortue.
facts.quote: Remains of the species are scarce, but subfossils have been discovered in caves on the Plaine Corail and in Caverne Tortue.

facts.statement: Julian Hume suggested in 2007 that Leguat's mention of green and blue parrots could refer to both the Rodrigues parrot and Newton's parakeet, or represent color morphs of the parakeet.
facts.quote: As Leguat mentioned both green and blue parrots in the same sentence, the British palaeontologist Julian Hume suggested in 2007 that these could either be interpreted as references to both the Rodrigues parrot and Newton's parakeet, or as two colour morphs of the latter.

facts.statement: Samuel Pasfield Oliver doubted in 1891 that the parrots mentioned by Leguat were the Rodrigues parrot, suggesting they were actually Newton's parakeet due to size differences.
facts.quote: In a footnote in an 1891 edition of Leguat's memoir, the British writer Samuel Pasfield Oliver doubted that the parrots mentioned were the Rodrigues parrot, due to their smaller size, and suggested they may have been Newton's parakeet.

facts.statement: The Rodrigues parrot is classified as a member of the tribe Psittaculini, though its closest relative among other species is unclear.
facts.quote: It is unclear to which other species it is most closely related, but it is classified as a member of the tribe Psittaculini, along with other Mascarene parrots.

facts.statement: British ecologists Anthony S. Cheke and Hume proposed that Mascarene parrots, like the dodo, may have derived from South Asian ancestors.
facts.quote: Many endemic Mascarene birds, including the dodo, are derived from South Asian ancestors, and the British ecologist Anthony S. Cheke and Hume have proposed that this may be the case for all the parrots there as well.

facts.statement: In 1893, E. Newton and Hans Gadow found the Rodrigues parrot closely related to the broad-billed parrot but could not determine if they belonged in the same genus due to missing crest evidence.
facts.quote: In 1893, E. Newton and the German ornithologist Hans Gadow found the Rodrigues parrot to be closely related to the broad-billed parrot due to their large jaws and other osteological features, but were unable to determine whether they both belonged in the same genus, since a head-crest was only known from the latter.

facts.statement: Graham S. Cowles found the skulls of the Rodrigues parrot and broad-billed parrot too dissimilar to be close relatives in 1987.
facts.quote: The British ornithologist Graham S. Cowles instead found their skulls too dissimilar for them to be close relatives in 1987.

facts.statement: In 1967, ornithologist James Greenway suggested that the species N. borbonicus might have been an escaped pet lory rather than a wild bird.
facts.quote: In 1967, the American ornithologist James Greenway suggested that N. borbonicus may have been an escaped pet lory seen by Dubois

facts.statement: In 2007, Hume suggested that Rothschild mistakenly linked N. borbonicus to the Rodrigues parrot by incorporating Dubois's account into the latter's description.
facts.quote: In 2007, Hume suggested that Rothschild had associated N. borbonicus with the Rodrigues parrot because he had mistakenly incorporated Dubois's account into his description of the latter

facts.statement: The Rodrigues parrot was the largest parrot species on Rodrigues, characterized by a large head and long tail.
facts.quote: The Rodrigues parrot was described as being the largest parrot species on the island, with a big head and a long tail.

facts.statement: The Rodrigues parrot had plumage described as uniform green coloration.
facts.quote: Its plumage was described as being of uniform green colouration.

facts.statement: Due to introduced rats, the Rodrigues parrot frequented and nested on offshore islets where rats were absent.
facts.quote: Due to a large population of introduced rats on Rodrigues, the parrots, the Rodrigues starling, and the Rodrigues pigeon, frequented and nested on offshore islets, where the rats were absent.

facts.statement: In 1671, Pingré noted that the Rodrigues parrot was rare and considered popular game.
facts.quote: Pingré indicated in 1671 that local species were popular game, and found that the Rodrigues parrot was rare

facts.statement: The last known mention of the species was in 1761, and it likely became extinct shortly thereafter.
